positions/devotio-moderna-piety/name: Devotio Moderna and The Imitation of Christ
positions/devotio-moderna-piety/altNames: Brothers and Sisters of the Common Life
positions/devotio-moderna-piety/oneLine: A simple, interior, Christ-centred piety of daily self-examination, meditation on the life of Jesus and humble service, lived in common by lay people and canons without monastic vows.
positions/devotio-moderna-piety/coreClai: Imitating Christ’s humility matters more than learned speculation.
Daily methodical meditation and examination of conscience form the soul.
Lay communities can live a devout common life in the world.
Copying and reading devotional books nourish the inner life.
positions/devotio-moderna-piety/keyTexts: Thomas à Kempis, The Imitation of Christ
positions/devotio-moderna-piety/origin: Founded by Geert Groote at Deventer (from c.1374) and spread through the Brothers and Sisters of the Common Life and the Windesheim congregation in the Low Countries and Germany; The Imitation of Christ (c.1418-27) was its classic text.
positions/devotio-moderna-piety/stronges: It made serious devotion accessible to lay people.
It nurtured educational reform (schools at Deventer, where Erasmus studied).
Its book has fed Catholics and Protestants alike.
Critics call it individualistic and anti-intellectual.
Protestant readers warn that "imitation" can eclipse justification by grace; Catholic critics found its lay communities irregular.
positions/devotio-moderna-piety/response: Admirers note that The Imitation is saturated with Scripture and grace, and that it was printed by Protestants (in adapted form) and Catholics for centuries.
positions/devotio-moderna-piety/conseque: Preparation for both Reformation piety and Catholic reform (Ignatius read it at Manresa).
positions/ignatian-spirituality/oneLine: Through the Spiritual Exercises, imaginative contemplation of the Gospels and the discernment of spirits, one learns to choose freely what serves the greater glory of God and to find God in all things.
positions/ignatian-spirituality/coreClai: Humans are created to praise, reverence and serve God (Principle and Foundation).
Imaginative contemplation places one within Gospel scenes.
Consolation and desolation are signs to be discerned (Rules for Discernment).
Contemplation leads to apostolic action: contemplatives in action.
positions/ignatian-spirituality/origin: Born of Ignatius of Loyola’s conversion (1521) and experiences at Manresa (1522), written as the Spiritual Exercises (approved 1548) and spread by the Society of Jesus (1540).
positions/ignatian-spirituality/stronges: It gives a practical, flexible method for discernment and decision-making.
It honours imagination and emotion as places where God works.
Jansenists and others accused Jesuits of laxity; Protestants saw the Exercises as works-centred.
Some critics worry that imagination and feeling can be mistaken for God’s voice.
positions/ignatian-spirituality/response: Ignatians answer that discernment is tested by Scripture, the Church and a director, and that the Exercises begin and end in grace.
positions/ignatian-spirituality/conseque: Modern retreat movement and spiritual direction, including among Protestants.
positions/carmelite-mysticism/name: Carmelite mysticism (Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross)
positions/carmelite-mysticism/oneLine: Prayer is friendship with God that grows through recollection, the prayer of quiet and purifying "dark nights" toward spiritual marriage; detachment from all that is not God prepares for union in love.
positions/carmelite-mysticism/coreClaims: Mental prayer is "an intimate sharing between friends" (Teresa).
The soul progresses through dwelling places toward union.
God purifies the soul through active and passive nights of sense and spirit.
True mystical experience bears fruit in humility, obedience and service.
positions/carmelite-mysticism/keyTexts/3: John of the Cross, Ascent of Mount Carmel; Dark Night; Spiritual Canticle
positions/carmelite-mysticism/origin: Arose in the 16th-century reform of the Carmelite order in Spain by Teresa of Ávila (from 1562) and John of the Cross (from 1568), under scrutiny from the Inquisition; continued by Thérèse of Lisieux and Edith Stein.
positions/carmelite-mysticism/proponents: Edith Stein (Teresa Benedicta of the Cross)
positions/carmelite-mysticism/strongestA: It offers the most detailed map of growth in prayer.
Teresa and John are Doctors of the Church.
It treats suffering and spiritual dryness with deep pastoral wisdom.
positions/carmelite-mysticism/strongestO: Contemporaries suspected illuminism (alumbrados); the Inquisition examined Teresa’s Life.
Protestant critics see stages of ascent as works-oriented and extra-biblical.
Some modern readers find its asceticism severe.
positions/carmelite-mysticism/responses/: Carmelites stress that everything is grace and that the dark night is God’s loving work, not human achievement.
positions/puritan-meditation/oneLine: Disciplined, Scripture-saturated meditation, secret prayer, family worship, diary-keeping and self-examination apply doctrine to the heart so that the believer grows in assurance and holiness.
positions/puritan-meditation/coreClaims/: Meditation "digests" Scripture and sermons, moving truth from head to heart.
Secret and family prayer and the Sabbath are daily and weekly disciplines.
Self-examination tests the reality of grace.
Heavenly-mindedness gives strength for present duty.
positions/puritan-meditation/origin: Developed among English and New England Puritans c.1600-1700 in manuals by Lewis Bayly, Joseph Hall, Richard Baxter, Thomas Watson and Isaac Ambrose; continued in evangelical devotion.
positions/puritan-meditation/strongestAr: It joins Word and Spirit, doctrine and experience.
It builds daily discipline into ordinary lay life.
It shaped evangelical quiet times and journalling.
positions/puritan-meditation/strongestOb: Critics say it encouraged anxious introspection.
Catholic and Orthodox observers note that it borrowed medieval methods while denying their sources.
positions/puritan-meditation/responses/0: Puritans insisted introspection must lead to Christ, not to the self, and wrote much on consolation.
positions/heart-religion-pietist-moravia: Pietist and Moravian heart religion
Herzensreligion
Moravian piety
Blood-and-wounds devotion
True Christianity is a living, felt relationship with the Saviour: conversion of the heart, joyful love for the crucified Christ, small-group fellowship, singing and continuous prayer.
Faith is a matter of the heart, not merely of doctrine.
Devotion centres on the wounds and love of the crucified Lamb.
Bands and choirs (small groups) foster confession and mutual care.
Continuous prayer and mission express the heart’s love (the Herrnhut 24-hour prayer watch from 1727).
Ezekiel 36:26
Galatians 2:20
Revelation 5:6-12
Zinzendorf, discourses; Moravian Daily Watchwords (Losungen, from 1731)

Grew out of Spener’s Pietism and the Halle movement, and was intensified at Herrnhut under Count Zinzendorf after the "Moravian Pentecost" of 13 August 1727, which began a hundred-year prayer watch and Moravian missions (1732).
Peter Böhler
August Gottlieb Spangenberg
Gerhard Tersteegen
It renewed warmth and joy in Protestant faith.
Its prayer watch fuelled pioneering missions.
It decisively influenced John Wesley.
Lutheran and Methodist critics (including Wesley) objected to "stillness" teaching and emotional excess during the "sifting time" (1740s).
Some found its blood-and-wounds imagery morbid.
Others feared feeling would replace Word and sacrament.
Zinzendorf himself corrected excesses after 1750, and Moravians kept strong sacramental and liturgical life.
Moravian missions; Methodist class meetings; modern evangelical heart language.
positions/quaker-silence-inward-prayer/o: Friends gather in expectant silence, without set liturgy or clergy, waiting on the inward light of Christ, and speak only when moved by the Spirit.
positions/quaker-silence-inward-prayer/c: Christ is present to teach his people himself.
Outward forms (liturgy, sacraments, paid ministry) are unnecessary; worship is inward.
Any member may be moved to minister, women equally with men.
Silence and stillness allow discernment of the Spirit’s leading.
positions/quaker-silence-inward-prayer/o: Arose with George Fox and the Children of the Light in northern England (1652) amid the radicalism of the Commonwealth.
positions/quaker-silence-inward-prayer/s: It trusts Christ’s promise to be present where two or three gather.
It gave equal voice to women and lay people.
Its silence has attracted seekers across traditions.
Other Protestants accused early Quakers of elevating the inner light above Scripture.
Rejection of outward sacraments contradicts Jesus’ commands for most churches.
Later liberal Quakerism moved, critics say, away from Christ-centred faith.
positions/quaker-silence-inward-prayer/r: Early Friends held that the Spirit who gave the Scriptures never contradicts them; many Friends remain explicitly Christian.
positions/quaker-silence-inward-prayer/c: Quaker testimonies of peace, equality and simplicity.
Influence on contemplative practice and silence in other churches.
positions/wesleyan-means-of-grace/name: Wesleyan means of grace and methodical piety
positions/wesleyan-means-of-grace/oneLin: God ordinarily gives grace through appointed means, prayer, searching the Scriptures, the Lord’s Supper, fasting and Christian conference, which seekers and believers alike should use, together with works of mercy, on the way to perfect love.
positions/wesleyan-means-of-grace/coreCl: Outward means are "ordinary channels" of preventing, justifying and sanctifying grace.
Seekers should not "be still" and wait for faith but use the means.
Constant communion and accountable small groups (class and band meetings) build holiness.
Grace aims at love of God and neighbour: Christian perfection.
positions/wesleyan-means-of-grace/keyTex: Wesley, Sermon 16 "The Means of Grace"; "The Duty of Constant Communion"
positions/wesleyan-means-of-grace/origin: Shaped in the Oxford Holy Club (1729), John Wesley’s Aldersgate experience (1738) and his break with Moravian "stillness" (1740), and organised in Methodist societies, classes and bands.
positions/wesleyan-means-of-grace/strong: It holds together sacrament, Scripture, prayer, accountability and social action.
It answers both formalism and enthusiasm.
Its small groups spread rapidly among the poor.
Calvinist evangelicals worried it encouraged works-righteousness and perfectionism.
Anglicans of the time accused Methodists of enthusiasm and irregularity.
Later Holiness movements arguably shifted emphasis from means to crisis experience.
positions/wesleyan-means-of-grace/respon: Wesley insisted the means have no power in themselves and that grace alone saves.
positions/wesleyan-means-of-grace/conseq: Methodist class meeting; hymn-singing (Charles Wesley); Holiness movement.
positions/charismatic-prayer/oneLine: The Spirit prays through believers in tongues, prophecy and healing prayer; worship is expectant, embodied and participatory, with prayer for the sick, deliverance and personal encounter.
positions/charismatic-prayer/coreClaims/: Praying in tongues edifies and expresses what words cannot (Romans 8:26; 1 Corinthians 14:2, 14).
Prayer expects God to act now in healing and power.
Worship involves the body: raised hands, dancing, falling, weeping.
All believers may minister in the Spirit’s gifts.
positions/charismatic-prayer/origin: Spread from Azusa Street (1906) and parallel revivals in Wales, India and Korea; entered historic churches through the charismatic renewal (1960) and the Catholic charismatic renewal (1967); now characteristic of much Global South Christianity.
positions/charismatic-prayer/strongestAr: It recovers New Testament expectation of the Spirit’s gifts.
It is at the heart of Christianity’s growth in the Global South.
positions/charismatic-prayer/strongestOb: Cessationists deny that tongues and prophecy continue.
Critics warn of emotionalism, manipulation and unbiblical phenomena.
Contemplatives and liturgical Christians sometimes find it noisy and experience-driven.
positions/charismatic-prayer/responses/0: Charismatics answer that Paul regulates rather than forbids gifts and that fruit (love, holiness) tests experiences.
positions/charismatic-prayer/consequence: Global Pentecostalism; 24-hour prayer movements; healing ministries.
